tagline.text: A pine-ridge traverse from Kayapa to Itogon

location.label: Location
location.text: Border of Kayapa (Nueva Vizcaya) and Tinongdan, Itogon (Benguet)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,500~4,000 (traverse, per person in a group of 10)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Manila Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) or Baguio Loakan Airport (BAG)

children.text: Mount Ugo is a peak of about 2,150 m between Kayapa in Nueva Vizcaya and Itogon in Benguet. The most popular route is a two-day traverse of about 32~33 km from Kayapa to Tinongdan, Itogon, with pine ridges, highland villages and a sea of clouds.

Mount Ugo (locally spelled Mt. Ugu) straddles the border of Nueva Vizcaya and Benguet. Its summit height varies by source. One trip report says the summit marker reads 2,220 m, hiking blogs and the Itogon tourism office give roughly 2,150~2,200 m, and a measured value of 2,086 m is also cited. So think of it as "about 2,150 m". It lies on the southern flank of the Cordillera range, like Mount Pulag, but is far less crowded, which makes it popular with hikers who want a quieter outing.

The best-known way to climb it starts in Kayapa, Nueva Vizcaya, crosses the summit and descends to Tinongdan in Itogon, Benguet. The whole trail is about 32~33 km and is usually walked in two days. On day one you climb from Kayapa through Indupit village to the Domolpos saddle; on day two you reach the summit in the early morning, then descend a long way through Lusod village to Tinongdan. A same-day out-and-back from Tinongdan is also possible, at about 13 km each way with roughly 1,400 m of elevation gain, which suits strong hikers.

The trail mostly follows pine forest, ridgelines and farm paths between highland villages. On clear days you can see Mount Pulag and the ranges toward Baguio, and at dawn clouds fill the valleys. Because you walk through places where people live, courtesy matters: close wooden gates behind you and greet villagers. Among hikers it is seen as a next step for those who have already done Pulag and want a moderate-to-hard traverse. Two suggestions for first-timers. First, the usual plan is an overnight bus from Manila that arrives at dawn and has you walking right away, so sleep on the bus as much as you can. Second, the second-day descent is about 16 km and tends to run late, so book your Baguio–Manila bus with some margin. Long photo and rest stops can make you finish later than expected.

The mountain also has a sad history. On June 26, 1987, Philippine Airlines Flight 206 (an HS 748) flying from Manila to Baguio crashed into the slopes of Mount Ugo in fog, killing all 50 people on board. A memorial marker for the crash is reported to stand in the mossy forest below the summit on the traverse. Please pass quietly and respectfully.

This is the signature route, about 32~33 km over two days. Climbs, a long descent, villages, mossy forest and pine ridges alternate, so the scenery keeps changing. Hiking sites rate it about 5 out of 9 ("major climb").

blocks.title: Sunrise and sea of clouds at the summit

children.text: Sleep at the Domolpos saddle, wake around

on day two and walk, and you reach the summit around sunrise. On clear days clouds spread across the valleys and the ridges toward Mount Pulag come into view. Mobile signal usually reaches the area near the summit.

Near the summit, straight pines stretch skyward, and on the way down you pass damp, moss-covered forest. Leeches can be present in the mossy forest, so tuck your trouser cuffs into your socks and use repellent.

You pass villages such as Indupit, Domolpos and Lusod and see the daily life of mountain residents up close. Many villages have little electricity, so nights are very dark and the stars are bright. Village schools and homes sometimes help with lodging, meals and water, so many hikers respect local circumstances and leave a small thank-you.
A marker for the 1987 crash is said to stand in the forest below the summit. Ask your guide for the exact location.
As you near Tinongdan there is a hanging bridge over the Agno River that marks the end of the long descent. Trip reports often end the hike near this bridge.

Recommended only for strong hikers in stable dry-season weather. Darkness falls early, so a headlamp is essential.

A 2026 guide gives about ₱1,000 one way for the bus, while older reports list ₱350~400, so fares differ greatly by period. Check the latest fare when booking.
The Aritao–Kayapa road is winding, so bring motion-sickness medicine.
Buses and vans to Kayapa reportedly leave from Dangwa Terminal and similar spots from about
. The fare is given as about ₱120~150 (2016 report).
To reach Tinongdan, go from Baguio through Itogon by jeep. Groups usually charter a "monster jeep" for the return to Baguio.
A chartered jeep from Tinongdan to Baguio is given as about ₱3,000 (₱300 per person for a group of 10).
The Baguio–Manila bus is about ₱600, and Sunday night is full, so book 3 days ahead.

The dry season, November to April, is the safe choice. From November to February dawn temperatures are very low and a sea of clouds often appears; from February to April it is relatively warm and often clear.
In the rainy season trails become slippery and muddy, and jeeps may not reach the villages, so you walk more. Some reports mention burnt pines from forest fires in hot years.
Local reports recommend November–February or February–April. In any month, check trail conditions and construction with a contact in Kayapa or Itogon before leaving.

There are no hotels on the mountain. During the traverse you usually sleep in the Domolpos elementary school building or at a saddle campsite. You must bring your own tent (a double-wall windproof one is recommended), sleeping bag and warm clothing. Many villages have little or no electricity, and mobile phones may not work at camp.
Meals are arranged with village households or carried yourself. There are no ATMs in Kayapa or Indupit, so bring cash. Back in Baguio, food and lodging are easy to find in the city.

Resting a day in Baguio before heading up softens the fatigue of the overnight bus from Manila. After the traverse, a jeep from Tinongdan back to Baguio and a meal and rest around Session Road is an easy plan. Snacks such as chocolate, nuts and energy bars, plus rice balls for lunch, are hard to buy in the villages, so prepare them in Manila or Kayapa.
Register at the Kayapa police station before entering, and arrange your guide and jeep in advance with the Itogon tourism contact at Tinongdan.
Domolpos is the last place to refill water before the summit, and there is no water on top. Also fill at least
at Lusod.
The long descent is hard on the knees. Trekking poles and knee supports help.
Victory Liner buses are very cold, so keep a windbreaker within easy reach.
If you open a wooden gate, always close it. Keep your voice down on village paths.
Carry out all your trash. The mountain shows fire scars, so be extremely careful with fire.
The Baguio–Manila bus on Sunday evening is full. Book in advance.
Bring a rain cover for your pack, a rain jacket and spare socks. Fog and showers soak clothes easily.
Phones may not work at camp, so agree on a meeting time and place with your group beforehand.
Fog and rain make the trail slippery and it is very cold near the summit. Do not enter without a guide. Fees and registration rules change often, so check the latest notices before departure.
Leeches can be present in the mossy forest section.
At night Domolpos is windy and temperatures drop to about 6~10℃.
A 2026 guide mentions road construction between Tinongdan and Lusod, which can lengthen travel time.
In the rainy season jeeps may not reach the villages.
The summit elevation differs by source, so the exact value cannot be guaranteed.
One of the highest peaks of the Cordillera to the northeast; some hikers combine it with Mount Ugo in one traverse.
The base city where the jeep brings you back from Tinongdan, with easy lodging and food.
Mummy sites north of Benguet that can be combined with a Pulag-area trip.
